claim: VHH123 is specific for mouse TfR.
source: Two anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) nanobodies, VHH123 specific for mouse TfR and VHH188 specific for human TfR, were used to track transplants non-invasively by PET/CT in mouse models, without the need for genetic modification of the transferred cells.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of VHH123.

claim: VHH188 is specific for human TfR.
source: Two anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) nanobodies, VHH123 specific for mouse TfR and VHH188 specific for human TfR, were used to track transplants non-invasively by PET/CT in mouse models, without the need for genetic modification of the transferred cells.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of VHH188.

claim: Anti-TfR nanobodies can track transplants non-invasively by PET/CT without genetic modification of transferred cells.
source: Two anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) nanobodies, VHH123 specific for mouse TfR and VHH188 specific for human TfR, were used to track transplants non-invasively by PET/CT in mouse models, without the need for genetic modification of the transferred cells.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Chelation of 89Zr and 64Cu radioisotopes to anti-TfR nanobodies results in radioisotope release upon endocytosis.
source: We provide a comparison of the specificity and kinetics of the PET signals acquired when using nanobodies radiolabeled with 89Zr, 64Cu, and 18F, and find that the chelation of the 89Zr and 64Cu radioisotopes to anti-TfR nanobodies results in radioisotope release upon endocytosis of the radiolabeled nanobodies.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract based on experimental comparisons.

claim: VHH188 detects Tfrchu/hu bone marrow transplants in C57BL/6 recipients by PET/CT.
source: We used a knock-in mouse that expresses a TfR with a human ectodomain (Tfrchu/hu) as a source of bone marrow for transplants into C57BL/6 recipients and show that VHH188 detects such transplants by PET/CT.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this experimental result.

claim: VHH123 can image C57BL/6 bone marrow transplanted into Tfrchu/hu recipients.
source: Conversely, C57BL/6 bone marrow and B16.F10 melanoma cell line transplanted into Tfrchu/hu recipients can be imaged with VHH123.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this experimental result.

claim: VHH123 can image B16.F10 melanoma cells transplanted into Tfrchu/hu recipients.
source: Conversely, C57BL/6 bone marrow and B16.F10 melanoma cell line transplanted into Tfrchu/hu recipients can be imaged with VHH123.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this experimental result.

claim: VHH188 produces an intense signal in the placenta of C57BL/6 mice impregnated by Tfrchu/hu males.
source: In C57BL/6 mice impregnated by Tfrchu/hu males, we saw an intense VHH188 signal in the placenta, showing that TfR-specific VHHs accumulate at the placental barrier but do not enter the fetal tissue.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this observation from PET/CT imaging.

claim: TfR-specific VHHs accumulate at the placental barrier but do not enter fetal tissue.
source: In C57BL/6 mice impregnated by Tfrchu/hu males, we saw an intense VHH188 signal in the placenta, showing that TfR-specific VHHs accumulate at the placental barrier but do not enter the fetal tissue.
evidence: The abstract states this as an interpretation of the placental imaging data.

claim: Anti-TfR radiotracers do not show observable accumulation in the CNS by PET/CT.
source: We were unable to observe accumulation of the anti-TfR radiotracers in the central nervous system (CNS) by PET/CT but showed evidence of CNS accumulation by radiospectrometry.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the negative PET/CT finding.

claim: Anti-TfR radiotracers show evidence of CNS accumulation by radiospectrometry.
source: We were unable to observe accumulation of the anti-TfR radiotracers in the central nervous system (CNS) by PET/CT but showed evidence of CNS accumulation by radiospectrometry.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this positive finding from radiospectrometry.

claim: The model can track transplanted cell types that express TfR by PET/CT.
source: The model presented here can be used to track many transplanted cell types by PET/CT, provided cells express TfR, as is typically the case for proliferating cells such as tumor lines.
evidence: The abstract states this as a conclusion about the utility of the model.

claim: Proliferating cells typically express TfR.
source: The model presented here can be used to track many transplanted cell types by PET/CT, provided cells express TfR, as is typically the case for proliferating cells such as tumor lines.
evidence: The abstract states this as established knowledge.

claim: Non-invasive tracking of specific cell types in vivo is a desirable goal in biomedical research, particularly in immunology and cancer.
source: Non-invasive tracking of specific cell types in vivo is a desirable goal in many fields of biomedical research, particularly as it pertains to immunology and cancer.
evidence: The introduction states this as a motivation for the research.

claim: Knowledge of biodistribution of immune cells and tumor cells is essential to monitor therapeutic interventions.
source: Knowledge of the biodistribution of immune cells and/or tumor cells in a disease model is essential to monitor therapeutic interventions.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: Fluorescence and luminescence-based methods suffer from absorbance and dispersal of emitted light.
source: Fluorescence and luminescence-based methods suffer from absorbance and dispersal of emitted light (Yoon et al., 2022), which limits the depth at which images of acceptable resolution can be obtained.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this limitation.

claim: Absorbance and dispersal of emitted light limits the depth at which fluorescence and luminescence methods can obtain acceptable resolution.
source: Fluorescence and luminescence-based methods suffer from absorbance and dispersal of emitted light (Yoon et al., 2022), which limits the depth at which images of acceptable resolution can be obtained.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this limitation.

claim: Fluorescence-based methods with multi-photon microscopy provide cellular resolution.
source: Fluorescence-based methods in conjunction with multi-photon microscopy provide cellular resolution, but usually require invasive surgery to gain access to the cells of interest (Choi et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this capability.

claim: Fluorescence-based methods with multi-photon microscopy usually require invasive surgery to access cells of interest.
source: Fluorescence-based methods in conjunction with multi-photon microscopy provide cellular resolution, but usually require invasive surgery to gain access to the cells of interest (Choi et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this limitation.

claim: SPECT and PET do not suffer from the drawbacks of fluorescence-based methods.
source: Methods that rely on the use of radioisotopes, such as single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and positron emission tomography (PET) do not suffer those drawbacks.
evidence: The introduction states this as a comparative advantage.

claim: SPECT and PET lack the resolution of optical microscopy.
source: While SPECT and PET lack the resolution of optical microscopy, they have the advantage of being non-invasive, quantitative, and enabling whole-body imaging in small animals at a resolution of ~1 mm, or a 1 microliter volume, for PET (Serkova et al., 2021) and even lower than 1 mm for SPECT (van der Have et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this limitation.

claim: SPECT and PET are non-invasive, quantitative, and enable whole-body imaging.
source: While SPECT and PET lack the resolution of optical microscopy, they have the advantage of being non-invasive, quantitative, and enabling whole-body imaging in small animals at a resolution of ~1 mm, or a 1 microliter volume, for PET (Serkova et al., 2021) and even lower than 1 mm for SPECT (van der Have et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support these advantages.

claim: PET has a resolution of ~1 mm or 1 microliter volume in small animals.
source: While SPECT and PET lack the resolution of optical microscopy, they have the advantage of being non-invasive, quantitative, and enabling whole-body imaging in small animals at a resolution of ~1 mm, or a 1 microliter volume, for PET (Serkova et al., 2021) and even lower than 1 mm for SPECT (van der Have et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this resolution specification.

claim: SPECT has a resolution lower than 1 mm.
source: While SPECT and PET lack the resolution of optical microscopy, they have the advantage of being non-invasive, quantitative, and enabling whole-body imaging in small animals at a resolution of ~1 mm, or a 1 microliter volume, for PET (Serkova et al., 2021) and even lower than 1 mm for SPECT (van der Have et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this resolution specification.

claim: SPECT and PET are finding increasing use in tumor immunology.
source: These methods are finding increasing use in the field of tumor immunology, as they can provide a whole-body image, unlike other approaches.
evidence: The introduction states this as an observed trend.

claim: Current PET/CT cell tracing methods require the use of a cell-specific tracer.
source: Current PET/CT cell tracing methods require the use of a cell-specific tracer.
evidence: The introduction states this as a characteristic of current methods.

claim: Cell-specific tracers typically rely on detection of an endogenous surface marker specific for cells of interest.
source: This typically relies on the detection of an endogenous surface marker that is specific for the cells of interest (Cao et al., 2019), or by genetically engineering cells of interest to enable their visualization, for example through expression of a viral kinase of unique specificity (Gambhir et al., 2000), or by introduction of a surface marker that can be selectively visualized (Minn et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this approach.

claim: Cells can be genetically engineered to express a viral kinase of unique specificity for visualization.
source: This typically relies on the detection of an endogenous surface marker that is specific for the cells of interest (Cao et al., 2019), or by genetically engineering cells of interest to enable their visualization, for example through expression of a viral kinase of unique specificity (Gambhir et al., 2000), or by introduction of a surface marker that can be selectively visualized (Minn et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this approach.

claim: Cells can be genetically engineered to introduce a surface marker that can be selectively visualized.
source: This typically relies on the detection of an endogenous surface marker that is specific for the cells of interest (Cao et al., 2019), or by genetically engineering cells of interest to enable their visualization, for example through expression of a viral kinase of unique specificity (Gambhir et al., 2000), or by introduction of a surface marker that can be selectively visualized (Minn et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this approach.

claim: VHHs (nanobodies) are enjoying increasing use for generation of immuno-PET tracers.
source: VHHs, also termed nanobodies, are enjoying increasing use for the generation of immuno-PET tracers that yield images of a quality superior to what is achieved using regular, intact immunoglobulins (Harmand and Islam, 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this trend.

claim: Nanobodies yield images of quality superior to intact immunoglobulins.
source: VHHs, also termed nanobodies, are enjoying increasing use for the generation of immuno-PET tracers that yield images of a quality superior to what is achieved using regular, intact immunoglobulins (Harmand and Islam, 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this comparative advantage.

claim: Nanobodies are recombinantly expressed variable fragments (VH) of heavy chain-only immunoglobulins produced by camelids.
source: Nanobodies are the recombinantly expressed variable fragments (VH) of heavy chain-only immunoglobulins produced by camelids (Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993; Ingram et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this definition.

claim: Nanobodies have a small size of ~15 kDa.
source: Their small size (~15 kDa), superior tissue penetration, specificity, affinity, and much shorter circulatory half-life compared to intact immunoglobulins make nanobodies excellent tracers for in vivo imaging.
evidence: The introduction states this as a characteristic of nanobodies.

claim: Nanobodies have superior tissue penetration compared to intact immunoglobulins.
source: Their small size (~15 kDa), superior tissue penetration, specificity, affinity, and much shorter circulatory half-life compared to intact immunoglobulins make nanobodies excellent tracers for in vivo imaging.
evidence: The introduction states this as a comparative advantage.

claim: Nanobodies have a much shorter circulatory half-life compared to intact immunoglobulins.
source: Their small size (~15 kDa), superior tissue penetration, specificity, affinity, and much shorter circulatory half-life compared to intact immunoglobulins make nanobodies excellent tracers for in vivo imaging.
evidence: The introduction states this as a comparative characteristic.

claim: Nanobodies are excellent tracers for in vivo imaging.
source: Their small size (~15 kDa), superior tissue penetration, specificity, affinity, and much shorter circulatory half-life compared to intact immunoglobulins make nanobodies excellent tracers for in vivo imaging.
evidence: The introduction states this as a conclusion based on nanobody properties.

claim: The transferrin receptor (TfR; CD71) is encoded by Tfrc.
source: The transferrin receptor (TfR; CD71; encoded by Tfrc) is a homodimeric type-II transmembrane protein that is near-ubiquitously expressed, in particular on proliferating cells (Kawabata, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this molecular identity.

claim: TfR is a homodimeric type-II transmembrane protein.
source: The transferrin receptor (TfR; CD71; encoded by Tfrc) is a homodimeric type-II transmembrane protein that is near-ubiquitously expressed, in particular on proliferating cells (Kawabata, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this structural description.

claim: TfR is near-ubiquitously expressed, particularly on proliferating cells.
source: The transferrin receptor (TfR; CD71; encoded by Tfrc) is a homodimeric type-II transmembrane protein that is near-ubiquitously expressed, in particular on proliferating cells (Kawabata, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this expression pattern.

claim: TfR is expressed on many tumor cells with variability depending on tumor type and differentiation status.
source: This includes many tumor cells with some variability depending on the tumor type and differentiation status (Ryschich et al., 2004; Faulk et al., 1980; Daniels et al., 2012; Basuli et al., 2017; Rychtarcikova et al., 2017; Kindrat et al., 2016; Horniblow et al., 2017; Shirakihara et al., 2022; Prutki et al., 2006).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references to support this expression pattern.

claim: TfR binds to and endocytoses iron (Fe+++)-loaded transferrin (Tf).
source: The TfR binds to and endocytoses iron (Fe+++)-loaded transferrin (Tf).
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge about TfR function.

claim: Tf remains bound to TfR in endosomal compartments where low pH releases Fe+++ cargo.
source: Tf remains bound to the TfR in endosomal compartments, where the resident low pH releases the Fe+++ cargo and thus converts Tf into apoTf, which remains TfR-bound at endosomal pH.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge about TfR trafficking.

claim: TfR-bound apoTf returns to the cell surface where TfR releases apoTf at neutral pH.
source: From there, TfR-bound apoTf returns to the cell surface, where the TfR releases apoTf at neutral pH.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge about TfR recycling.

claim: TfR is expressed by endothelial cells that line the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
source: TfR is also expressed by endothelial cells that line the blood-brain barrier (BBB) for delivery of Fe+++-loaded transferrin to the central nervous system by transcytosis.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge about TfR expression.

claim: TfR delivers Fe+++-loaded transferrin to the CNS by transcytosis.
source: TfR is also expressed by endothelial cells that line the blood-brain barrier (BBB) for delivery of Fe+++-loaded transferrin to the central nervous system by transcytosis.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge about TfR function at the BBB.

claim: The nanobodies used in this study bind TfR and can traverse the BBB.
source: The nanobodies used in this study bind TfR and can traverse the BBB (Wouters et al., 2020; Wouters et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this capability.

claim: Mouse embryos critically depend on iron supply in the form of Tf captured from maternal circulation.
source: Mouse embryos critically depend on an iron supply in the form of Tf captured from the maternal circulation, delivered to the embryo via the TfR expressed on the syncytiotrophoblast-I (Sangkhae and Nemeth, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this developmental requirement.

claim: Tf is delivered to the embryo via TfR expressed on syncytiotrophoblast-I.
source: Mouse embryos critically depend on an iron supply in the form of Tf captured from the maternal circulation, delivered to the embryo via the TfR expressed on the syncytiotrophoblast-I (Sangkhae and Nemeth, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this delivery mechanism.

claim: Whether nanobodies can traverse the placenta and reach the embryo has not been explored.
source: Whether the small size of nanobodies allows them by analogy with the BBB- to traverse the placenta and reach the embryo has not been explored.
evidence: The introduction states this as a knowledge gap.

claim: VHH123 is also termed Nb62.
source: We use two nanobodies: VHH123 (also termed Nb62 Wouters et al., 2020) and VHH188, which recognize the murine TfR and the human TfR (TFRC), respectively.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this alternative nomenclature.

claim: VHH123 recognizes murine TfR.
source: We use two nanobodies: VHH123 (also termed Nb62 Wouters et al., 2020) and VHH188, which recognize the murine TfR and the human TfR (TFRC), respectively.
evidence: The introduction states this as a defining characteristic.

claim: VHH188 recognizes human TfR (TFRC).
source: We use two nanobodies: VHH123 (also termed Nb62 Wouters et al., 2020) and VHH188, which recognize the murine TfR and the human TfR (TFRC), respectively.
evidence: The introduction states this as a defining characteristic.

claim: Tfrchu/hu mice express a TfR with a human TfR ectodomain.
source: We use these VHHs together with a knock-in mouse model that expresses a TfR with a human TfR ectodomain (Tfrchu/hu) (Wouters et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this mouse model description.

claim: VHH123 allows detection of cells of mouse origin transplanted into Tfrchu/hu mice.
source: VHH123 allows the detection of cells of mouse origin, such as bone marrow progenitors or tumor cells, transplanted into Tfrchu/hu mice.
evidence: The introduction states this as a key application.

claim: VHH188 can track primary cells from Tfrchu/hu mice after transfer into wild-type mice.
source: Conversely, we use VHH188 to track primary cells from Tfrchu/hu mice after transfer into wild-type mice.
evidence: The introduction states this as a key application.

claim: This is the first immuno-PET study on localization of TfR in mouse embryos in live mice.
source: We report the first immuno-PET study on localization of the TfR in mouse embryos in live mice.
evidence: The introduction states this as a novel contribution.

claim: 89Zr and 64Cu are released from imaging agents upon binding TfR due to internalization and exposure to low endosomal pH.
source: We find that 89Zr and 64Cu, ligated to these TfR-specific VHHs by non-covalent chelation, are released from the imaging agent upon binding the TfR, due to internalization and exposure to low endosomal pH.
evidence: The introduction states this as a key finding.

claim: Release of free 89Zr and 64Cu from imaging agents are factors to consider when using these over extended periods.
source: The release of free 89Zr and 64Cu from imaging agents are factors to consider when using these over extended periods of time.
evidence: The introduction states this as a practical consideration.

claim: Covalent modification of VHHs with 18F avoids release of free radioisotope.
source: Covalent modification of VHHs with 18F avoids the release of free radioisotope, but the short half-life of 18F limits the observation window to <12 hr.
evidence: The introduction states this as an advantage of 18F labeling.

claim: The short half-life of 18F limits the observation window to <12 hr.
source: Covalent modification of VHHs with 18F avoids the release of free radioisotope, but the short half-life of 18F limits the observation window to <12 hr.
evidence: The introduction states this as a limitation of 18F labeling.

claim: The Tfrchu/hu mouse line has been deposited at Jackson Laboratories as strain 038212.
source: At most, crossing of a mouse model of interest with the Tfrchu/hu mouse line would be required (deposited at Jackson Laboratories, strain 038212).
evidence: The introduction states this as information about resource availability.

claim: VHH123 and VHH188 bind only to their appropriate TfR with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface-expressed proteins by immunoblot.
source: We show that both VHHs bind only to the appropriate TfR, with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface-expressed proteins by immunoblot, LC/MSMS analysis of immunoprecipitates, SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins and flow cytometry (Figure 1; Table 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section references figures and tables showing experimental data.

claim: VHH123 and VHH188 bind only to their appropriate TfR with no obvious cross-reactivity by LC/MSMS analysis.
source: We show that both VHHs bind only to the appropriate TfR, with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface-expressed proteins by immunoblot, LC/MSMS analysis of immunoprecipitates, SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins and flow cytometry (Figure 1; Table 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section references figures and tables showing experimental data.

claim: VHH123 and VHH188 bind only to their appropriate TfR with no obvious cross-reactivity by SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins.
source: We show that both VHHs bind only to the appropriate TfR, with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface-expressed proteins by immunoblot, LC/MSMS analysis of immunoprecipitates, SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins and flow cytometry (Figure 1; Table 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section references figures and tables showing experimental data.

claim: VHH123 and VHH188 bind only to their appropriate TfR with no obvious cross-reactivity by flow cytometry.
source: We show that both VHHs bind only to the appropriate TfR, with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface-expressed proteins by immunoblot, LC/MSMS analysis of immunoprecipitates, SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins and flow cytometry (Figure 1; Table 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section references figures and tables showing experimental data.

claim: Virtually all contaminants co-immunoprecipitated with the VHHs were of cytoplasmic and nuclear localization.
source: Virtually all contaminants that were co-immunoprecipitated were of cytoplasmic and nuclear localization (Table 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section references a table showing LC/MS/MS data.

claim: Cytoplasmic and nuclear proteins are not accessible to anti-TfR nanobodies in an in vivo setting.
source: This is of minor concern, as these proteins are not accessible to our anti-TfR nanobodies in an in vivo setting.
evidence: The results section states this as an interpretation of the contamination data.

claim: Injection of VHH123-based conjugate into Tfrchu/hu mice yielded signal exclusively in kidneys, considered non-specific.
source: Injection of the VHH123-based conjugate into Tfrchu/hu mice yielded a signal exclusively in the kidneys, which we consider a non-specific signal (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: 89Zr radiolabeled VHHs typically accumulate in kidneys in the absence of a specific target.
source: 89Zr radiolabeled VHHs typically accumulate in the kidneys in the absence of a specific target.
evidence: The results section states this as established knowledge.

claim: Injection of VHH188-based conjugate into C57BL/6 mice yielded strong PET signal only in kidneys, considered non-specific.
source: Similarly, injection of the VHH188-based conjugate into C57BL/6 mice likewise yielded a strong PET signal only in the kidneys (Figure 3B), again considered non-specific accumulation of the tracer.
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: Properly matched VHH-mouse combinations produced intense PET signal localizing to bones at 48 hr post-injection.
source: For the properly matched VHH-mouse combinations (89Zr radiolabeled VHH123 conjugate injected into C57BL/6 mice; 89Zr radiolabeled VHH188-conjugate injected into Tfrchu/hu mice), each produced an intense PET signal that localizes to bones, mainly the vertebrae, sacrum, coxal bone as well as both epiphyses of the femur and the proximal epiphysis of the humerus at 48 hr post-radiotracer injection (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: The results section references figures showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: Mean activity measured by PET was significantly different between matched and unmatched VHH/mouse pairs in liver, spleen, femoro-tibial articulation, and spleen by ROI analysis.
source: The mean activity measured by PET was significantly different between matched and unmatched VHH/mouse pairs in the liver, spleen, femoro-tibial articulation (knee), and spleen, by region of interest (ROI) analysis (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The results section references figures showing ROI analysis data.

claim: The pattern of label distribution is better explained by sequestration of free 89Zr in mineralized bone and cartilage than by bone marrow uptake.
source: While the signals from long bone extremities and vertebrae suggest uptake of the anti-TfR radioconjugate by bone marrow (Zimmer et al., 2011), presumably due to the high demand for iron required for erythropoiesis (Richard and Verdier, 2020), this pattern of label distribution is better explained by sequestration of free 89Zr in mineralized bone and cartilage (Raavé et al., 2019; Abou et al., 2011) (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section cites references and references a figure to support this interpretation.

claim: The weak signal from femur diaphyses relative to vertebral column and bone extremities suggests free 89Zr accumulation in mineralized bone predominates.
source: The weak signal from the diaphyses of the femora relative to the intense signal in the vertebral column and bone extremities suggests that accumulation of free 89Zr in mineralized bone predominates under these conditions.
evidence: The results section states this as an interpretation of imaging patterns.

claim: Several tissues showed significant differences in activity between matched and unmatched mouse/VHH pairs at 72 hr post-injection, particularly brain, spleen, small intestine, and liver.
source: Several tissues showed significant differences in activity between the matched and unmatched mouse/VHH pairs: particularly in the brain, spleen, small intestine, and liver.
evidence: The results section states this based on ex vivo measurements.

claim: Femur bones flushed of bone marrow retained very strong activity in matched conditions, confirming deposit of free 89Zr in bone matrix.
source: Femur bones flushed of all bone marrow retained a very strong activity in the matched conditions – showing that the mineral bone retains a high activity when depleted of bone marrow (>200,000 CPM/bone) – confirming the deposit of free 89Zr in the bone matrix.
evidence: The results section states this based on ex vivo measurements.

claim: Flushed bone marrow showed activity significantly higher in matched vs. unmatched conditions.
source: Nevertheless, flushed bone marrow showed activity (20,000–30,000 CPM/flushed bone) that was significantly higher in the matched vs. unmatched conditions (Figure 3G).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing ex vivo measurements.

claim: At later timepoints, strong PET signals in long bone extremities are due in part to bone marrow accumulation but predominantly to free 89Zr in mineralized bone matrix.
source: We conclude that at later timepoints, the strong PET signals in the long bone extremities (femur, tibia, and humerus) are due in part to bone marrow accumulation of anti-TfR radiolabeled VHHs, but predominantly so to accumulation of free 89Zr in the mineralized bone matrix.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion from the data.

claim: No obvious accumulation of tracer was seen in brain parenchyma by PET.
source: No obvious accumulation of tracer was seen in brain parenchyma by PET, but significant differences of activity were found in the ex vivo analysis (Figure 3H), in line with the reported ability of VHHs that recognize the TfR to deliver bound materials across the blood-brain barrier (Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The results section references a figure and cites a reference.

claim: Significant differences of brain activity were found in ex vivo analysis.
source: No obvious accumulation of tracer was seen in brain parenchyma by PET, but significant differences of activity were found in the ex vivo analysis (Figure 3H), in line with the reported ability of VHHs that recognize the TfR to deliver bound materials across the blood-brain barrier (Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing ex vivo measurements.

claim: VHHs that recognize TfR can deliver bound materials across the blood-brain barrier.
source: No obvious accumulation of tracer was seen in brain parenchyma by PET, but significant differences of activity were found in the ex vivo analysis (Figure 3H), in line with the reported ability of VHHs that recognize the TfR to deliver bound materials across the blood-brain barrier (Wouters et al., 2020).
evidence: The results section cites a reference to support this capability.

claim: Failure to detect adequate PET signal in brain is due to comparatively small amounts of anti-TfR VHH crossing the BBB.
source: The failure to detect a PET signal of adequate strength in the brain are due to the comparatively small amounts of anti-TfR VHH that cross the BBB.
evidence: The results section states this as an interpretation.

claim: Previous PET images with VHHs recognizing CD8, Ly6C/G, or CD11b showed no accumulation of 89Zr in skeletal elements.
source: When analyzing PET images obtained with VHHs that recognize targets other than the TfR, which includes VHHs that recognize CD8 (Rashidian et al., 2017), Ly6C/G (Pishesha et al., 2022), or CD11b (Priem et al., 2020), as examined previously, no accumulation of 89Zr in skeletal elements was seen.
evidence: The results section cites references to support this comparison.

claim: Lack of bone signal in mismatched anti-TfR VHH/mouse pairs leads to conclusion that free 89Zr is released only when VHH binds its respective TfR.
source: These previous observations, combined with the lack of any bone signal in the mismatched anti-TfR VHH/mouse pairs, lead us to conclude that free 89Zr is released from the VHH-conjugates in vivo, but only when the VHH binds to its respective TfR.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Chelation of 89Zr to DFO depends on its charge.
source: Because chelation of 89Zr to DFO depends on its charge (Imura et al., 2021), we hypothesized that binding of VHH-89Zr conjugates to the appropriate TfR delivers them to endosomal compartments of low pH, where 89Zr is then released from the DFO moiety.
evidence: The results section cites a reference to support this mechanism.

claim: 89Zr is freed from VHH123-PEG-DFO at pH <5.6 in vitro.
source: We examined release of 89Zr from the VHH123-PEG-DFO construct in vitro by exposure to low pH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). 89Zr is freed from the adduct at pH <5.6, which is well within the pH range of late endosomal compartments (Cain et al., 1989).
evidence: The results section references a figure and cites a reference.

claim: pH <5.6 is within the pH range of late endosomal compartments.
source: 89Zr is freed from the adduct at pH <5.6, which is well within the pH range of late endosomal compartments (Cain et al., 1989).
evidence: The results section cites a reference to support this pH range.

claim: At 1 hr post-injection, a strong PET signal is observed in femur diaphyses, epiphyses, coxal bones, and sacrum (bone marrow) for all three isotopes.
source: At 1 hr post-injection of the 89Zr, 64Cu, or 18F-labeled radiotracer, we observe a strong PET signal in the diaphyses and both epiphyses of the femora and in the coxal bones and sacrum (bone marrow), thus showing that VHH123 accumulates specifically at those locations, and that the signal is not simply due to free radioisotope only (Figure 4).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: VHH123 accumulates specifically in bone marrow locations at 1 hr post-injection.
source: At 1 hr post-injection of the 89Zr, 64Cu, or 18F-labeled radiotracer, we observe a strong PET signal in the diaphyses and both epiphyses of the femora and in the coxal bones and sacrum (bone marrow), thus showing that VHH123 accumulates specifically at those locations, and that the signal is not simply due to free radioisotope only (Figure 4).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: 89Zr and 64Cu radiolabeled VHH123 accumulated in the spleen at 1 hr post-injection.
source: 89Zr and 64Cu radiolabeled VHH123 also accumulated in the spleen.
evidence: The results section states this observation.

claim: The 18F-based imaging agent provided a sharper picture than 89Zr and 64Cu agents.
source: The 18F-based imaging agent provided a sharper picture, with some signal originating from the gut and gall bladder, typically seen when using 18F-based radiotracers comprising bulky hydrophobic moieties, in this case a TCO-Tetrazine clicked product (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: The results section cites a reference to support this observation.

claim: 18F-based radiotracers comprising bulky hydrophobic moieties typically show signal in gut and gall bladder.
source: The 18F-based imaging agent provided a sharper picture, with some signal originating from the gut and gall bladder, typically seen when using 18F-based radiotracers comprising bulky hydrophobic moieties, in this case a TCO-Tetrazine clicked product (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: The results section cites a reference to support this typical pattern.

claim: The 18F signal had fully decayed at 12 hr timepoint due to short half-life.
source: At the 12 hr timepoint the 18F signal had fully decayed due to the short half-life of 18F.
evidence: The results section states this observation.

claim: Improved signal quality with 18F is offset by shorter half-life.
source: Improved signal quality is thus offset by the shorter half-life of 18F.
evidence: The results section states this as a trade-off.

claim: For 64Cu-based agent, bone marrow signal remains weakly visible at 24 hr post-injection.
source: For the 64Cu-based agent, the bone marrow signal remains weakly visible at 24 hr post-injection (Figure 5).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: Liver and gut signals increase at later timepoints for 64Cu-labeled tracer, attributed to slow release of 64Cu from NOTA to plasma proteins.
source: The liver and gut signals increase at later timepoints for the 64Cu-labeled tracer, a phenomenon attributable to a slow release of 64Cu from NOTA to plasma proteins such as albumin, which delivers copper to the liver where it can then be conjugated to ceruloplasmin (Dearling et al., 2011; Mirick et al., 1999).
evidence: The results section cites references to support this mechanism.

claim: At 24 hr post-injection of 89Zr-labeled agent, signal is mostly from bone extremities and vertebrae, attributed to free 89Zr in mineralized bone.
source: In mice that received the 89Zr-labeled agent, we mostly observe a signal from the bone extremities and vertebrae at 24 hr post-injection, which we attribute to labeling of mineralized bone with free 89Zr with a minor contribution of a TfR-specific bone marrow signal.
evidence: The results section states this as an interpretation of imaging data.

claim: A pair of punctiform signals in anterior cranium appear prominently with 18F tracer, tentatively attributed to incisor root accumulation.
source: For all imaging agents, we observe a pair of punctiform signals in the anterior region of the cranium. These appear very prominently with the 18F tracer, and at later timepoints -but less clearly- with the 89Zr and 64Cu imaging agents, potentially explained by the lower positron emission range of 18F. Limited by the resolution of the CT images, we tentatively attribute these signals to the accumulation of the radiotracer in the roots of the incisors, where iron uptake is required for proper amelogenesis (McKee et al., 1987).
evidence: The results section cites a reference and states this as a tentative interpretation.

claim: Iron uptake is required for proper amelogenesis in incisor roots.
source: Limited by the resolution of the CT images, we tentatively attribute these signals to the accumulation of the radiotracer in the roots of the incisors, where iron uptake is required for proper amelogenesis (McKee et al., 1987).
evidence: The results section cites a reference to support this biological requirement.

claim: Internalization of 89Zr and 64Cu VHH123-based imaging agents leads to release of free radioisotope responsible for most signal at 24 hr or later.
source: We conclude that internalization of 89Zr and 64Cu VHH123-based imaging agents leads to release of free radioisotope (89Zr and 64Cu), which is responsible for most of the signal detected at later (24 hr or later) timepoints and thus does not truly reflect distribution of the TfR itself at those timepoints.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion from the data.

claim: ROI analysis shows shift of PET signal distribution towards liver with 64Cu-labeled VHH123 at later timepoints.
source: This is particularly clear from a ROI analysis of the liver and knee PET signals, when normalized to the average kidney signal (Figure 5B), that shows a shift of distribution of PET signal towards the liver with 64Cu-labeled VHH123 and towards the knee for 89Zr-labeled VHHs at later timepoints post-injection.
evidence: The results section references a figure showing ROI analysis.

claim: ROI analysis shows shift of PET signal distribution towards knee for 89Zr-labeled VHHs at later timepoints.
source: This is particularly clear from a ROI analysis of the liver and knee PET signals, when normalized to the average kidney signal (Figure 5B), that shows a shift of distribution of PET signal towards the liver with 64Cu-labeled VHH123 and towards the knee for 89Zr-labeled VHHs at later timepoints post-injection.
evidence: The results section references a figure showing ROI analysis.

claim: Release of 89Zr or 64Cu from imaging agents is unavoidable consequence of binding to proper targets.
source: Combined, these results establish specificity of recognition of the respective VHHs for their intended targets. Moreover, the results show that release of 89Zr or 64Cu from the imaging agents is the unavoidable consequence of their binding to the proper targets.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion.

claim: Choice of isotopes for anti-TfR nanobodies must be made with respect to tissues to be visualized and time scale of experiment.
source: The choice of isotopes for conjugation to anti-TfR nanobodies must, therefore, be made with respect to the tissue(s) that are to be visualized, as well as the time scale of the experiment (~3–5 isotope half-lives).
evidence: The results section states this as a practical recommendation.

claim: At 2 weeks post bone marrow transplantation, 24 hr after VHH123-PEG-DFO-89Zr injection, transferred cells are observed in spleen and femoral bone.
source: At 2 weeks post bone marrow transplantation, 24 hr after injection of VHH123-PEG-DFO-89Zr, the presence of the transferred cells in the marrow is observed in the spleen and femoral bone, together with a strong signal from free 89Zr accumulation in the bone matrix (Figure 6A).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: Spleen signal appeared more prominent in bone marrow transplant recipients than in wild-type C57BL/6 mice at 24 hr post-injection.
source: The signal in the spleen appeared more prominent than that observed when imaging wild-type C57BL/6 mice at 24 hr post-injection of the same VHH, as pointed out through ROI analysis (Figure 6F vs. Figure 5B), which could reveal the presence of hematopoietic bone marrow in the spleen.
evidence: The results section references figures showing ROI analysis.

claim: Images at 1 hr post VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr injection show powerful signal in spleen, interpreted as bone marrow engraftment.
source: Strikingly, the images acquired at 1 hr post VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr injection show a powerful signal in the spleen, something not observed when imaging Tfrchu/hu mice with the same radiotracer, which can be easily interpreted as the presence of bone marrow engraftment in the spleen (Figure 6C and G).
evidence: The results section references figures showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr was unable to show engraftment of C57BL/6 bone marrow in isogenic recipient.
source: As a control, VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr was unable to show engraftment of C57BL/6 bone marrow cells in an isogenic recipient (Figure 6D and G).
evidence: The results section references figures showing control experiment data.

claim: Imaging Tfrchu/hu recipients immediately after C57BL/6 bone marrow transplantation reveals only faint signal in knee and liver.
source: Indeed, imaging of Tfrchu/hu recipient mice immediately after C57BL/6 bone marrow transplantation using VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr reveals only a faint signal in the knee and liver (Figure 6E).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: Timing of tracer injection and PET imaging is critical to avoid confounding effect of free 89Zr bone matrix signal.
source: Specific tracing of TfR-positive cells of mouse or human origin is thus possible when using VHH123 or VHH188 as the tracer in a Tfrchu/hu or wild-type recipient, respectively. Depending on the mass of TfR+ cells present the recipients, timing of tracer injection and the PET imaging session is critical to avoid the confounding effect of the free 89Zr bone matrix signal.
evidence: The results section states this as a practical consideration.

claim: The study establishes feasibility of detecting transplanted bone marrow cells and their hematopoietic descendants amidst invisible recipient cells.
source: These data establish the feasibility of detecting transplanted bone marrow cells and their hematopoietic descendants amidst populations or recipient cells that remain invisible to the imaging agent used.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion.

claim: At 2 weeks post-inoculation, VHH123-PEG-NOTA-64Cu did not yield clear signal in lungs of B16.F10-bearing mice.
source: Imaging done at 2 weeks post-inoculation of the B16F10 tumor did not yield a clear signal in the lungs (Figure 7A), as metastases typically arise some 3 weeks after injection for this number of cells.
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: B16.F10 metastases typically arise ~3 weeks after injection of 5×10^4 cells.
source: Imaging done at 2 weeks post-inoculation of the B16F10 tumor did not yield a clear signal in the lungs (Figure 7A), as metastases typically arise some 3 weeks after injection for this number of cells.
evidence: The results section states this as established knowledge.

claim: At 4 weeks post-transplantation, clear signal originating from lungs was observed in B16.F10-bearing mice.
source: At 4 weeks post-transplantation, we observed a clear signal originating from the lungs of the same mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: Non-specific anti-GFP VHHEnh-PEG-NOTA-64Cu showed only weak passive accumulation in lung metastases at 4 weeks.
source: To exclude the possibility of non-TfR-specific accumulation of radiotracer in necrotic tumor tissue, we injected tumor-bearing mice with a non-specific anti-GFP VHHEnh-PEG-NOTA-64Cu conjugate (Figure 7B and D), which showed only weak passive accumulation in the lung metastases at 4 weeks post-tumor cell infusion.
evidence: The results section references figures showing control experiment data.

claim: Necropsy confirmed presence of melanotic tumors in lungs of B16.F10-bearing mice.
source: At necropsy, we confirmed the presence of melanotic tumors in the lungs (Figure 7F), which were also visible on the lung CT.
evidence: The results section references a figure showing necropsy photographs.

claim: VHH123 gave significantly higher signal in whole lungs by ROI analysis.
source: By ROI analysis of the PET signals, VHH123 gave a significantly higher signal in the whole lungs (Figure 7G).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing ROI analysis.

claim: PET signal from B16.F10 metastases correlates well with dense tumor tissue on CT.
source: The PET signal from B16.F10 metastases in the lung correlates well with what appears to be dense tumor tissue on the corresponding CT image.
evidence: The results section states this as an observation.

claim: VHH123-PEG-NOTA-64Cu gave overall stronger signal in hyperdense lung tumor tissue than VHHEnh-PEG-NOTA-64Cu, though not significantly.
source: When performing ROI analysis restricted to the PET signal in hyperdense lung tumor tissue, VHH123-PEG-NOTA-64Cu gave an overall stronger signal when compared to VHHEnh-PEG-NOTA-64Cu, although not by a significant margin (Figure 7H).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing ROI analysis.

claim: ROI analysis on lung and heart is less precise due to breathing movements and beating heart during PET acquisition.
source: It is important to emphasize that ROI analysis on lung and heart is less precise, due to breathing movements and beating heart during acquisition of the PET signal.
evidence: The results section states this as a limitation.

claim: Anti-mouse TfR nanobody VHH123 is well-suited to track TfR-expressing cells of mouse origin in Tfrchu/hu recipient mice.
source: The anti-mouse TfR nanobody VHH123 is thus well-suited to track TfR-expressing cells of mouse origin in Tfrchu/hu recipient mice.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion.

claim: All proliferating cells express TfR, so any tumor or proliferating cell of mouse origin can be detected non-invasively without genetic modification.
source: Since all proliferating cells express TfR, in principle, any tumor or proliferating cell of mouse origin can be detected non-invasively without the need for genetic modification of the transplanted cells.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion.

claim: The congenic pair of mice with species-specific anti-TfR VHHs is a unique tool for transplant studies.
source: This congenic pair of mice, in combination with the species specificity of the anti-TfR VHHs, is thus a unique tool for studies of this type.
evidence: The results section states this as a conclusion.

claim: C57BL/6 females mated with Tfrchu/hu males produce heterozygous Tfrchu/wt embryos.
source: C57BL/6 females were mated with a Tfrchu/hu male or with a C57BL/6 male as a control. Embryos will thus be heterozygous for the presence of the two TfR isoforms.
evidence: The results section states the mating scheme and expected genotype.

claim: Proper mouse and human TfR homodimers will be formed in heterozygous embryos, possibly with interspecific hybrid TfR heterodimers.
source: We hypothesize that proper mouse and human TfR homodimers will be formed, in addition to the possible formation of the interspecific hybrid TfR heterodimer.
evidence: The results section states this as a hypothesis.

claim: Rapid uptake of VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr was observed in individual placentas of heterozygous Tfrchu/wt embryos.
source: Two weeks post-fertilization, the pregnant females were injected retro-orbitally with VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr. We observed rapid uptake of the VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr radiotracer in the individual placentas of the heterozygous (Tfrchu/wt) embryos (Figure 8A).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: Wild-type C57BL/6 placentas were barely detectable with VHH188, showing much weaker signal.
source: Wild-type C57BL/6 placentas were barely detectable in females crossed with a C57BL/6 male, showing a much weaker signal (Figure 8B).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: The difference in placental signal between Tfrchu/wt and wild-type placentas is significant by ROI analysis.
source: This difference is significant through ROI analysis (Figure 8C).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing ROI analysis.

claim: Low but detectable VHH188 signal in wild-type placentas is attributed to possible cross-reactivity to mouse TfR at very high expression levels.
source: We attribute the low but detectable signal for VHH188 to possible cross-reactivity to the mouse TfR when expressed at the very high levels on syncytiotrophoblast-I: placental tissue expresses a much higher than average level of Tfr (Sangkhae and Nemeth, 2019; Cox et al., 2009).
evidence: The results section cites references and states this as an interpretation.

claim: Placental tissue expresses much higher than average level of Tfr.
source: We attribute the low but detectable signal for VHH188 to possible cross-reactivity to the mouse TfR when expressed at the very high levels on syncytiotrophoblast-I: placental tissue expresses a much higher than average level of Tfr (Sangkhae and Nemeth, 2019; Cox et al., 2009).
evidence: The results section cites references to support this expression pattern.

claim: Post-euthanasia dissection confirmed intense VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr signal originates from placenta and not embryo.
source: Post-euthanasia dissection and separation of the placenta from the embryo was done, followed by a separate round of PET/CT imaging of the extirpated uterus and the embryos it contained. This confirmed that the intense VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr signal originates from the placenta and not from the embryo (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: The results section references figures showing ex vivo imaging data.

claim: No signal corresponding to free 89Zr was seen in embryos or pregnant females despite intense placental labeling.
source: Notwithstanding intense labeling of the placenta, we did not see a signal that corresponds to free 89Zr in either embryos or in the pregnant female.
evidence: The results section states this as an observation.

claim: Placental imaging results depart from other imaging experiments which showed 89Zr release when appropriate target TfR was expressed.
source: This results, therefore, departs from what was seen for any of the other imaging experiments, all of which showed release of 89Zr when the appropriate target TfR was expressed.
evidence: The results section states this as a comparison.

claim: Placental signal was already quite intense at 1 hr post-injection of VHH188-PEG-DFO-89Zr.
source: Of note, the signal in the placenta was already quite intense at 1 hr post-injection of the radiotracer (Figure 8F).
evidence: The results section references a figure showing PET/CT imaging data.

claim: The ability to track transplanted cells non-invasively over time is useful for monitoring tumor growth in response to therapy and following fate of transplanted hematopoietic cells.
source: The ability to track the fate of transplanted cells non-invasively over time is a useful asset for several applications. These include the monitoring of tumor growth in response to various forms of therapy in a pre-clinical setting, or to follow the fate of transplanted cells of hematopoietic origin.
evidence: The discussion states this as a motivation.

claim: Current methods include luminescence-based approaches where transplanted cells express a luciferase reporter.
source: Methods currently in use include luminescence-based approaches, in which the transplanted cells are engineered to express a suitable reporter, such as a luciferase (Yoon et al., 2022; de Almeida et al., 2011).
evidence: The discussion cites references to support this current method.

claim: Luminescence methods do not provide cellular resolution.
source: Luminescence methods do not provide cellular resolution.
evidence: The discussion states this as a limitation.

claim: Fluorescence-based methods in multi-photon microscopy achieve single-cell resolution but typically involve invasive surgery.
source: Alternatively, to achieve single-cell resolution, fluorescence-based methods have been applied in multi-photon microscopy (Choi et al., 2015), but this typically involves invasive surgical interventions to expose the target tissue or organ, because absorption by surrounding tissue limits the depth of penetration of the excitation beam and emitted fluorescence.
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support this method and limitation.

claim: NMR lacks specificity to detect particular cell populations, though tumors exceeding certain size are readily visualized.
source: Non-invasive methods such as NMR lack the specificity to detect particular cell populations, although tumors that exceed a certain size are readily visualized (Serkova et al., 2021).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support this limitation.

claim: SPECT and PET can detect specific cell populations based on radiolabeled ligands but lack single-cell resolution.
source: SPECT and PET can detect specific cell populations based on the use of radiolabeled ligands that recognize them, but lack single-cell resolution.
evidence: The discussion states this as a characteristic.

claim: Most widely used radioisotopes for SPECT include 123I and 99Tc with half-lives of ~13 hr and ~6 hr respectively.
source: The most widely used radioisotopes for SPECT include 123I and 99Tc, with half-lives of ~13 hr and ~6 hr, respectively (Adak et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support these specifications.

claim: Radiolabeled immunoglobulins show excellent specificity but their molecular mass impedes tissue penetration and imposes long circulatory half-life.
source: Radiolabeled immunoglobulins used as imaging agents show excellent specificity, but their molecular mass (~150 kDa) impedes efficient tissue penetration and imposes a long circulatory half-life.
evidence: The discussion states this as a limitation.

claim: When using immunoglobulin-based imaging agents for PET, use of long-lived radioisotopes such as 89Zr is indicated.
source: When using immunoglobulin-based imaging agents for PET, the use of long-lived radioisotopes such as 89Zr (t1/2=~3.3 days) is, therefore, indicated.
evidence: The discussion states this as a practical consideration.

claim: Introduction of nanobodies for SPECT and PET overcomes many limitations of immunoglobulin-based imaging agents.
source: The introduction of nanobodies for SPECT and PET overcomes many of the limitations of immunoglobulin-based imaging agents.
evidence: The discussion states this as an advantage.

claim: Small size of nanobodies improves tissue penetration and drastically reduces circulatory half-life.
source: The small size of nanobodies improves tissue penetration and drastically reduces the circulatory half-life of nanobody-based imaging agents.
evidence: The discussion states this as an advantage.

claim: Free nanobodies are typically excreted via kidneys and have circulatory half-life of ~30 min.
source: Free nanobodies are typically excreted via the kidneys and have a circulatory half-life of ~30 min, versus a half-life (in mice) of several days for intact immunoglobulins (Oliveira et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support this half-life.

claim: Intact immunoglobulins have circulatory half-life of several days in mice.
source: Free nanobodies are typically excreted via the kidneys and have a circulatory half-life of ~30 min, versus a half-life (in mice) of several days for intact immunoglobulins (Oliveira et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support this half-life.

claim: Unbound nanobodies are rapidly cleared from circulation to yield improved signal-to-noise ratio.
source: This means that unbound nanobodies are rapidly cleared from the circulation to yield a much-improved signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: The discussion states this as an advantage.

claim: Conjugation of PEG20kDa moiety improves contrast by reducing renal clearance rate of nanobodies.
source: Conjugation of a PEG20kDa moiety further improves contrast by reducing somewhat the renal clearance rate of the nanobodies (Rashidian et al., 2016).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support this improvement.

claim: Chemo-enzymatic methods allow site-specific and reproducible modification of nanobodies with substituents including chelators and click handles.
source: Chemo-enzymatic methods for the modification of nanobodies allow their site-specific and reproducible modification with substituents of interest, including the installation of chelators for radiometals such as 89Zr and 64Cu, as well as click handles for site-specific covalent modification with 18F (Harmand and Islam, 2021).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support these methods.

claim: For tumor detection, xenografts in immunocompromised mice are widely used with tumor-specific imaging agents based on antibodies recognizing human-specific surface markers.
source: For detection of tumors, xenografts in immunocompromised mice are widely used in combination with tumor-specific imaging agents. Typically, they are based on antibodies that recognize human-specific surface markers (Freise and Wu, 2015).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference to support this approach.

claim: Methods for detection of tumors of mouse origin in their natural host are few and far between.
source: Methods for the detection of tumors of mouse origin in their natural host are few and far between.
evidence: The discussion states this as a knowledge gap.

claim: A combination of anti-TfR nanobodies and mice expressing either wild-type or humanized TfR may be used to trace different cell types in vivo that express TfR.
source: We show that a combination of anti-TfR nanobodies and mice that express either a wild-type (mouse) or a humanized TfR may be used to trace different cell types in vivo that express the TfR.
evidence: The discussion states this as a key finding.

claim: It is possible to track cells of mouse origin in humanized Tfrchu/hu mice and humanized Tfrchu/hu mouse bone marrow in C57BL/6 mice.
source: It is thus possible to track cells of mouse origin in humanized Tfrchu/hu mice and humanized Tfrchu/hu mouse bone marrow in C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: The discussion states this as a key finding.

claim: Mice carrying Tfrchu/wt fetuses showed strong signal for VHH188 in placenta, indicative of trans-endothelial transport.
source: Mice carrying Tfrchu/wt fetuses showed a strong signal for VHH188 in the placenta, indicative of trans-endothelial transport of the imaging agent.
evidence: The discussion states this as an interpretation of the data.

claim: At 14 days of gestation, no embryonic tissues other than TfR on syncytiotrophoblast-I showed accumulation of label.
source: Except for the TfR on syncytiotrophoblast-I, at 14 days of gestation, no other embryonic tissues showed any accumulation of label.
evidence: The discussion states this as an observation.

claim: The combination of human and mouse-specific anti-TfR VHHs with Tfrchu/hu mice constitutes a congenic pair ideally suited for transplant experiments.
source: The combination of human and mouse-specific anti-TfR VHHs with mice that were engineered to express a TfR with the human TfR ectodomain constitutes a congenic pair of mice ideally suited for a variety of transplant experiments.
evidence: The discussion states this as a conclusion.

claim: Growth of tumors of mouse origin transplanted into Tfrchu/hu mice can be followed non-invasively in response to treatments.
source: The growth of tumors of mouse origin, when transplanted into Tfrchu/hu mice, can be followed non-invasively, for example, in response to various treatments.
evidence: The discussion states this as a potential application.

claim: Human patient-derived tumor xenografts can be followed upon transplantation into mice without genetic modification, even without tumor-specific antibodies.
source: Conversely, human patient-derived tumor xenografts (PDX models) can be followed upon transplantation into mice without a requirement for genetic modification of the transplant, even if no tumor-specific antibodies are available.
evidence: The discussion states this as a potential application.

claim: Transplantation of C57BL/6-isolated tissues and tumor cells in Tfrchu/hu is straightforward as both are of same genetic background.
source: Transplantation of C57BL/6-isolated tissues and tumor cells (-lines) in Tfrchu/hu is straightforward, as both recipient and graft are of the same genetic background.
evidence: The discussion states this as an advantage.

claim: The only neo-epitope of the graft would be the TfR ectodomain, considered negligible risk for immune rejection.
source: The only required neo-epitope of the graft would be the ectodomain of the TfR, which we consider a negligible risk for immune rejection: the Tfrchu/hu mouse expresses a chimeric TfR protein where only aminoacids 196–381 of the mouse TfR are replaced with the homologous aminoacids of the human TfR, that have a 74% pairwise identity by alignment using Clustal Omega (Wouters et al., 2022; Madeira et al., 2024).
evidence: The discussion cites references and states this as an interpretation.

claim: Tfrchu/hu mouse expresses chimeric TfR where only amino acids 196–381 of mouse TfR are replaced with homologous human TfR amino acids with 74% pairwise identity.
source: The only required neo-epitope of the graft would be the ectodomain of the TfR, which we consider a negligible risk for immune rejection: the Tfrchu/hu mouse expresses a chimeric TfR protein where only aminoacids 196–381 of the mouse TfR are replaced with the homologous aminoacids of the human TfR, that have a 74% pairwise identity by alignment using Clustal Omega (Wouters et al., 2022; Madeira et al., 2024).
evidence: The discussion cites references to support this molecular description.

claim: Lack of obvious PET signal in CNS may be due to proteins traversing BBB accumulating at concentration far lower than blood plasma.
source: The lack of an obvious PET signal in the CNS when imaging mice may be due to the fact that proteins that traverse the BBB, such as the TfR nanobody conjugates, accumulate in the CNS at a concentration far lower (around 1–5%) than that in blood plasma (Pothin et al., 2020; Meier et al., 2022).
evidence: The discussion cites references to support this explanation.

claim: 89Zr radioconjugates are prone to radioisotope release post-internalization, which is first step of transcytosis required for BBB crossing.
source: Furthermore, 89Zr radioconjugates are prone to radioisotope release post-internalization, which is the first step of transcytosis required for plasma proteins to traverse the BBB.
evidence: The discussion states this as an explanation.

claim: Both 89Zr and 64Cu radioconjugates were PEGylated, which may impede transcytosis.
source: Finally, both the 89Zr and 64Cu radioconjugates were PEGylated, which may impede transcytosis.
evidence: The discussion states this as a potential limitation.

claim: Non-PEGylated 18F radioconjugates might circumvent transcytosis issues, but short half-life may not allow adequate CNS visualization.
source: While the use of non-PEGylated 18F radioconjugates might circumvent these issues, their short circulatory and isotopic half-life may not allow the visualization at adequate sensitivity of a signal in the CNS.
evidence: The discussion states this as speculation about potential approaches.

claim: Gamma ray spectrometry confirmed accumulation of both nanobodies in CNS of appropriate genotype compared to controls.
source: Even so, gamma ray spectrometry on various organs from mice that received 89Zr-conjugated anti-TfR tracers confirmed accumulation of both nanobodies in the CNS of the appropriate genotype compared to control conditions (Figure 3H).
evidence: The discussion references a figure showing gamma ray spectrometry data.

claim: Release of free 89Zr and 64Cu by nanobody conjugates was surprising and unique to anti-TfR VHHs.
source: Release of free 89Zr and 64Cu by the nanobody conjugates was a surprising observation, unique to the anti-TfR VHHs.
evidence: The discussion states this as a notable finding.

claim: For no other 89Zr-labeled, PEGylated VHH has such striking and rapid release of free 89Zr been seen.
source: For no other 89Zr-labeled, PEGylated VHH have we seen such a striking and rapid release of free 89Zr.
evidence: The discussion states this as a comparison to previous work.

claim: Osteophilic properties of 89Zr have been well documented.
source: The osteophilic properties of 89Zr have been well documented (Raavé et al., 2019; Abou et al., 2011) and confirmed in our hands (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The discussion cites references and references a figure to support this property.

claim: Signal generated by free 89Zr should not be confused with localization of anti-TfR nanobody to spinal cord, bone marrow, or skeletal elements.
source: The signal generated by free 89Zr should, therefore, not be confused with the localization of anti-TfR nanobody to the spinal cord, bone marrow, or skeletal elements more generally.
evidence: The discussion states this as a caution.

claim: Careful interpretation is required when examining bone marrow accumulation using anti-TfR-89Zr conjugates or any internalizing 89Zr-labeled tracer.
source: Careful interpretation is required when examining accumulation of tracer in bone marrow when using anti-TfR-89Zr conjugates or any other internalizing 89Zr-labeled tracer.
evidence: The discussion states this as a recommendation.

claim: Observed release was unique to anti-TfR VHHs and seen only in presence of appropriate target, consistent with mechanism targeting DFO-89Zr chelate in TfR-localized compartments.

claim: Despite strong placental accumulation, no sign of free 89Zr release was seen in pregnancy experiments.
source: Notwithstanding the very strong accumulation of label seen in the placenta, which we ascribe to the presence of the human-ectodomain modified TfR at the surface of the embryonic syncytiotrophoblast-I, we did not see any sign of release of free 89Zr.

claim: The former explanation is favored because it would allow delivery of Fe+++ to embryonic tissues.
source: We favor the former explanation because it would allow delivery of Fe+++ to embryonic tissues and satisfy their demand for iron.
